blocks.x: This is a project carried out by the students at Southwestern Louisiana Institute with the cooperation of several of the faculty members. The students at Southwestern and these faculty members are very much interested in getting facts concerning the musical life of Mr. Lawrence Dewey,

one of the jazz greats of America. Mr. Dewey, how did you become interested in music, and where did, why and when did you get your start? Well, I got my start while young in La Place, and my brother had a band, the orchestra, and one of the fellas got out there that played guitar that made me jump on a guitar and I began to play by myself by air. You know, it was an air band. So we got, I got so good that, that we organized the kid over a band there, and we left from there, came to New Orleans. Well, Mr. Dewey, what about your family musical life? Well, they all played ordinary music in those days. They all pick up somehow or another. They managed to play together,
and I followed. What were some of the instruments that you, what were some of the instruments that your people in your family played? Did everybody play every instrument? Oh, my, one of my brothers

played, one played violin, one played bass violin, one played trombone. My sister played aroha. My mother was a dancer. My grandmother was a singer. So that's the way. My daddy was a violin player also. Mr. Dewey, uh, what kind of music did you all play, uh, in your early age? Ragtime. Ragtime. Ragtime. Well, could you give us a little bit of information about ragtime in those days? Well, that's the only time
kind of music, type of music that was used at that time. Uh, did you take almost any music of the time

and ragtime in ragtime? Or was it some music which was especially written for you? Well, no, we, we, we rag all, all, all pieces. Mr. Dewey, did you all use any old popular favorites? Yes, we used, uh, quite a few, but I can't remember, memorize all, but, but taking the straw, I can remember, I remember taking the straw. Mr. Dewey, would you tell us
what happened when you decided to leave Laplace, and what happened, what kind of music did you meet

when you got to New Orleans? Well, when I got to New Orleans, I joined the Kid Ora Band before we left Laplace, and then that's where we met jazz. We used to go to hill jazz in New Orleans, and we finally pick it up.
Uh, feed them to us. Uh, Mr. Dewey, we'd like to know some of the, uh, famous pieces that, uh, Kid Ora's Band, which you were a member of, played when you got to New Orleans. Will you tell us some of
them? That's what I'll mention now. Decevris, Blue Tiger Rags, and such name. I featured that on my

clanness. All right. Tiger Rags, then, was one of your specialties, huh? Oh, yeah. St. Louis Blues. St. Louis Blues. St. Louis Blues. All right. Now, uh, what other numbers did you suggest? Just let it go on.

How about Maple Leaf Rag? Maple Leaf Rag? Well, uh, we played that, but not often. But... Denny Ramble? Denny Ramble, yeah. Well, what about the, uh, Beale Street Blues? Beale Street Blues, yeah. We played that, Rick. Rampart Street Parade?

Rampart Street Parade? South Rampart. South Rampart. South Rampart Street Parade. That's, they played that. How about High Society? High Society. Oh, yeah. High Society. Did Mr. Handy come to New Orleans at any time, uh, down there while your groups were
playing? Did he ever visit you? One time I met Mr. Handy, I took his job in Chicago. He was,
he beat me up there with his band, his orchestra. What do you mean by he beat you? Would you tell him? His orchestra was up there before mine was. Ah-ha. Do you know any of the
things that they played at that time? I do not know, but I did that. My piano player came to

Chicago with him, Lil. Lil was his name? Lil Hardin, Lil Armstrong's first player. Uh-huh. Lil Hardin, Louis Armstrong's first ride. Mr. Dewey, we'd like to know the various combinations of instruments that played, uh, for the various, uh, occasions that you people were hired in New Orleans. Would you tell us how many there were and generally what instruments played? Seven. Seven pieces.
All right. Trombone, trumpet, clarinet, piano, drum, and bass. Cut it off just for the minute.
Mr. Dewey, did they use both the banjo and the guitar in these combinations? When did they use both of them, or
when did they use them separately? Well, they didn't have, no, the orchestra I, I, I was with, never did use no guitar. They started off with banjo. Banjo was the first instrument to take out.

All right. Would you tell us if they had to substitute, uh, any instruments in their band, how did they go about getting substitute instruments? What do you mean, to replace the, the... Yes, that's right.
Well, then, then they'd use the guitar like that, to substitute the banjo.
Mr. Dewey, did they ever use the tuba, the big bass horn, in any of the combos that you played with?

No, nothing, none, no orchestra at all. I played with. Did you ever use any string instruments, uh, Mr. Dewey, with your groups? Yes, my, my guitar player, he substituted, he, he doubled up with violin.
Mr. Dewey, we'd like to know how many of the men in these, uh, groups that you played with

red music. They're all red except my, except I. I, the only one didn't read, but I played so good that the violin player Pierron, Mr. Pierron, offered to teach me for nothing. Good. Mr. Dewey, would you
tell us about the various jobs that you played, how you got them, and how you made arrangements for them?

Well, I'll tell you, the, the leader of the band usually have cards made, and, and a phone number. So naturally, when they want you, they phone you, that, uh, they got an engagement for you. Then the price is as usual, $2.75 a man. That's what you got in the night, but four hours work, from eight to 12.
Mr. Dewey, would you tell us the various place, places that your band played while you were in New Orleans?

Mr. Dewey, would you tell us the, uh, the band played? Among, among the, among the players, there's the 101 Wrench, uh, Pete Lawless Cabaret, and Nagel and Vor, Nagel and Hunt's Cabaret. There's three places right there, in the Storyville. Now, but I played at, uh, uh, Cardinal. Yeah, I played in the Blue Room, Roosevelt Hotel with A.J. Piron. I played at, uh, Racetrack. I played at Franchina. I played at, uh, West End. What about the Montelion? Montelion Hotel Blue Room. I also played, uh, that's right, go right ahead. I started at, I even played at Millenburg, and Old Lady Lee, both, both of the questions from New Orleans to Covington.
Oh. Uh, Mr. Dewey, did you play in other places outside of New Orleans, Mississippi, etc.? Do you recall any places that you played? Yeah, with some, someone else. I was only hired.
Meluxin, Mississippi, Brookhaven, Natchez.
Uh, Mr. Dewey, would you tell us something about playing for funerals in New Orleans? What kinds of, of instrumental groups played for the funeral?
Regular brass bands, 25, 30 piece bands.
Did you ever play in any of these brass bands, or any of your men play in these funeral bands?
I never did, but some, or a few of my men have, have, have played with them.
Whenever the band group played, did they go into the graveyard, uh, with the burial party near the grave?

Yes, I, uh, I remember sometimes they did. I don't know if they did at all times. Somebody would, they would go to the... Mm-hm. and when they were coming from the grave, they would play, I'd be glad when you're dead, you rascal you.
Mr. Deer, we wish you would tell us how you men went about getting arrangements to play in your band.

Well, we used to go from hall to hall sometimes where the band would orchestra be playing and each one would take us a number that could learn and we'd finally get a number down and the next day we'll go and rehearse that same number over.
Mr. Deer, when your band got through playing, did you fellas go out and meet with some of the other bands and have a jam session or what did you do?
Oh no, we went around 101 ranks to around 25 then. We all would gather together and have a little fun, play a pool and different things.
Mr. Deer, would you tell us some of the bands that you heard while you were out listening and tell us some of the groups that you may have played with?
Well, some of those I heard was Joe Robichaud, Papa Silasin, and the Eagle Band. I played with the Eagle Band myself.
And what are they now? Kid Ory.
Kid Ory. Kid Ory. King Oliver. King Oliver. King Oliver.
All right. Was there one other one?
What about the Hot Five? No, that wasn't out there.
Mr. Deer, we'd like for you to tell us, for instance, when these white musicians picked up jazz from the Cullen Boys.

Well, they used to come to those places nightly, and they got them so good so they'd say, Well, Deer, you want to take a walk around the block? I said, Yes. Go ahead. I'll rest you up. I'll play clarinet. And so the rest of the instruments, the other boys would rest them up like that. That's the way they started. Mr. Deer, when you were in the Warriors, did you happen to meet Buddy Bolger? I'm sure he must have run into him. Oh, yes. And New Orleans knows about him. There's no question to ask, because he started that jazz off himself. Well, Mr. Deer, let's go to Chicago now. We know you went there. What year did you go, and how did you go about getting up there? I mean, why did you go? Well, I'm going to tell you why. There's two booking agents came from Chicago down there in the red light district where I was playing at Pete Law on Murray and Bienville Street. And they heard my orchestra, and during the intermission, they found out I was to leave at the band, and they had to talk with me. Okay. Now, what year was that, Mr. Deer? You went to Chicago? 1917. 1917. Were there any other jazz bands up there before you? Yeah, there had quite a few. But then that there wasn't a station in Chicago, such as the Dixieland, Manuel Perez, the Creole Band, and I was about the fourth number there, but I hid it in Chicago and stayed there. And in fact, I signed my contract out in New Orleans right there for Chicago. Now, how about, when did King Oliver come? Was that before or after you? That's way after me. My first trumpet player died. And the other one I had, Mud Carey, came to New Orleans, and he said the climate was too cold, so he was marked second trumpet player, so he came to New Orleans and sent King Oliver in his place. He never did come back until King Oliver got to playing with me. Mr. Deer, will you tell us now something about the job situation there in Chicago, where you played and how much and things like that, how often you played? Well, I played at the Deluxe 35th State. That was my first job out of New Orleans. And my salary was $35 a week per man. The leader got $10 extra. Okay. I also played the Dreamland. I played the Royal Garden. What about the unions? What about the unions? You know, sometimes, were they? Oh, yeah. The walking delegates started seeking up the Lawrence, because I was raising too much sand up there. So I had to get in the union up there. Of course, that made a little difference in prices, so our prices up there was $35 a week. Did you consider that a lot more than New Orleans? Oh, yes. New Orleans was that $1750 orchestra. There was no union in the Orleans then? No. Mr. Dewey, I remember seeing a picture of your band in Jazzmen, the famous book on jazz, where you were playing for a World Series in Chicago. Will you tell us something about that? Yes, sir. That's 1919 World Series. That's between, scale between the White Sox and the Cincinnati Black Sox.
That's your only band.
That was the only band. That's the only colored band in history to play a World Series of the country.
Mr. Dewey, would you tell us some of the fine players that played with you or that you knew while you were in Chicago?

Well, I left New Orleans with Sugar Johnny, and he got in bad health, and I switched to Mud Carry. After Mud Carry, the climate was too cold. He dropped me in Chicago, came back to New Orleans and sent King Oliver with me. So King Oliver stuck with me a while later, then he sent Armstrong later. Mr. Dewey, what did you think about Armstrong? I mean, as much as you know about him, what do you think about him? Greatest. One in the world greatest. Do you like his style of playing? Oh, yes. I really do. Did he play any different style from what they have played in New Orleans? New Orleans style? Oh, yes. Was jazz changing at that point? Was it changing to a, in a different, was it a different form, or was it still the same old Dixieland? The same, the same old Dixieland, but Armstrong added a little more to it. Now, Mr. Dewey, about the musicians in Chicago, did they come down and listen to you and learn jazz in that way? Is that the way they learned jazz? From one orchestra to another in New Orleans, they made all those nightclubs to be sure that when they'd go back they'd have an idea of what jazz was. In other words, they learned, they came down to New Orleans to find out about it. They didn't wait until you got to Chicago. No, indeed not. Mr. Dewey, did you have anybody especially that you admired as a player on your own instrument, like a clarinet player? Oh, yes. I admire Sidney Bershaw. In fact, he was with me and we fell out on that account because I read and he didn't read but he could outplay me.
Mr. Dewey, a while ago, we did not ask you any questions at all about your family background, but would you tell me, were your parents and were all the people in your family Catholic?
Yes, sir. They are really Catholic, everyone in my family.
All right. Now, Mr. Dewey, I'd like for you to tell us, if you will, how big a part Catholic musicians played in this growth of jazz in New Orleans. How many of the fellas down there were Catholics?
Mostly. Mostly, mostly the odd number were Catholics, I think, because I lived downtown and most everybody downtown was Catholic.
Mr. Dewey, did you and your group ever make any recordings of any kind?
No, not mine. King Oliver did, but I had to have with, I had to stop playing at that time.
Let it go. Mr. Dewey, have you ever written any pieces of music?
Yes, I wrote three and I still got them right here. They've been copyrighted and everything. The Evangeline Blues, I like to take my girls to the beach, and Lafayette Stomp.
Mr. Dewey, would you tell us about when you left Chicago? Did you get any other jobs in any other place? If so, what were some of these jobs?
Yes, I played cabaret work and I was also theatrical. I used to work on the off and circuit of the year, and you saw sessions. When was that?
What year was this? Well, all right. He doesn't know. Mr. Dewey, would you tell us about your coming back south, about what time you came back here and your reasons for coming back south?

For coming back south, I got in bad health up to Cunningham, and the doctor had ordered me to stop playing. So I came to New Orleans to rest up. while there, after I rest up for a while, Jack Carey asked me to come out to Lafayette to play a dollar excursion as one of the men had taken sick. So I came out here to Lafayette to play a one Sunday dollar excursion, and I've been around Lafayette since. Mr. Dewey, would you explain to Forest students who are young and don't know what is a dollar excursion? A dollar excursion is admission for each person on the train. A dollar. A dollar. Coming from New Orleans to Lafayette, round trip, dollar round trip. Good. Mr. Dewey, where did the band usually play on those dollar excursions? On a train. On a train in a baggage car. While you were in New Orleans, did you ever play in any of these wagons advertising boxing matches and river excursions and so forth? Oh, yes. We called that the back end that's sliding from on the base body and still on the tail end on the wagon. Still good. Mr. Dewey, what happened during Carnival? I'm sure there's a lot of activity then. Did you play in any of these parades? I remember seeing a lot of bands walking along with the Jefferson City Buzzards in some of those groups. Oh, yes. All clubs had some kind of a band. Of course, you didn't have, if you had a juice hop and a guitar, because all musicians get employed on Mardi Gras. Mr. Dewey, how is it you got to settle down here in Lafayette? What brought you over here? Well, I had an orchestra here from Crowley by the name of the Black Eagle. They heard me playing clarinet and the fellow talked to me and gave me such a good offer to stay down here, so I stayed in Lafayette. Now, when you say stayed, you mean that's when you came over in one of the dollar excursions. That's correct. Uh-huh, I see. Mr. Dewey, after you came over here, we would be interested in finding out what were some of the famous jazz bands of this area, colored jazz bands that were playing? Colored jazz bands, the Banner Banner in New Iberia, Black Eagle, Crowley, Claiborne William, Donaldson Villa, Tooth Johnson, Baton Rouge, Black Dead, Devil, Thibodeau. The Black Devils were originally from Plackman, that was a correction. Uh, you mentioned the Banner Band from New Iberia, now, Bunk Johnson was from there, did he play with that band, did you know Bunk? Yeah, Bunk and I joined the Banner Band about the same time when Bunk came from New Orleans to join the Banner Band. Most of the year. Uh, were any white bands playing jazz in this area around that time? I had a couple, I can remember, Frank Munts and Bill Landry. How'd it go? Well, mister, did you teach anybody playing the clarinet and who are these fellas? Yeah, I taught several boys. I taught a boy called Gobert, I taught him how to play trombone, the other one, Abraham Martin, I taught him about guitar, and Buster Banks, I taught him how to play saxophone. So you played all these instruments yourself? Yeah. Did you learn them all by written music or just pick them up by ear? Yeah. I pick them up myself. In other words, you weren't just, you weren't just confined to the clarinet, you played several, yeah. Did you ever play a saxophone or a trombone on a bandstand? Yeah, saxophone, all clarinet players play saxophone. Good. You told us all about your playing, when about was it that you quit playing and why did you quit? About 12 years now, I had to stop on a kind of bad hilt. Mister, Jimmy, do you miss the clarinet and sometimes wish that you could be back? Oh yes, I do miss it. Do you ever take out your clarinet by yourself and play for yourself just for fun? No, I just look at it. If I could play it, I'd be in with an orchestra. What you say you want to know? Well, Mr. Julian, I know I'm a young fella and a lot of us young boys would like to get a little bit of background on jazz. Could you give the guys and the girls an encouraging word on this jazz situation? Just say anything you'd like. Well, I know most of the, my friends used to teach at the student that they're all well acquainted with Professor Ogier. Don't you know Professor Ogier? No, not yet. I'm not there yet. I'm still a young guy. Oh, well. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
